items.stem: What is a displacement reaction?
options: A less reactive metal takes the place of a more reactive metal
A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound
items.answer: A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound
items.markingKey: The more reactive metal pushes the less reactive one out of its compound.

items.stem: Explain why the blue colour of copper sulfate solution fades when magnesium is added.
items.answer: Magnesium displaces the copper; blue copper ions are replaced by colourless magnesium ions in the solution.
items.markingKey: magnesium displaces copper [1]; blue copper compound replaced by colourless magnesium sulfate [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why silver does not react with copper sulfate solution.
items.answer: Silver is less reactive than copper, so it cannot displace copper from its compound.
items.markingKey: silver less reactive [1]; cannot displace [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei adds a piece of lead to iron sulfate solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs and explain your answer.
items.answer: No reaction, because lead is less reactive than iron.
items.markingKey: no reaction [1]; lead below iron in reactivity series [1] [2]

items.stem: Ines adds a piece of iron to copper sulfate solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs, explain why, write the word equation and describe what you would see.
items.answer: Yes: iron is more reactive than copper. iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper. Observation: a pink-brown coating of copper forms and the blue colour fades.
items.markingKey: reaction occurs with reason [1]; word equation [1]; observation [1] [3]

items.stem: Freya adds a piece of lead to zinc sulfate solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs and explain your answer.
items.answer: No reaction, because lead is less reactive than zinc.
items.markingKey: no reaction [1]; lead below zinc in reactivity series [1] [2]

items.stem: Mateo adds four metals, W, X, Y and Z, to solutions of each other’s salts. Results: metal W displaced X, Y, Z; metal X displaced Z; metal Y displaced X, Z; metal Z displaced none of the others. (a) Explain how you used the results to decide the order. (b) Explain why the experiment does not need a test of each metal with its own salt. (c) Suggest one other observation, apart from a coating forming, that shows a reaction has happened.
items.answer: (a) The metal that displaced the most others is the most reactive; the one that displaced none is the least reactive. (b) A metal cannot displace itself, so there would be no reaction and no information. (c) A temperature rise, or a change in the colour of the solution.
items.markingKey: (a) number of displacements [1]; most / none linked to order [1] [2] (b) A metal cannot displace itself, so there would be no reaction and no information [1] (c) A temperature rise, or a change in the colour of the solution [1]

items.stem: Amara adds four metals, W, X, Y and Z, to solutions of each other’s salts. Results: metal W displaced X, Z; metal X displaced none of the others; metal Y displaced W, X, Z; metal Z displaced X. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) The metals are copper, iron, lead, magnesium. Suggest which letter is which metal. (c) Explain why the experiment does not need a test of each metal with its own salt.
items.answer: (a) Y > W > Z > X (b) W = iron; X = copper; Y = magnesium; Z = lead (c) A metal cannot displace itself, so there would be no reaction and no information.
items.markingKey: (a) Y > W > Z > X [1]; Y > W > Z > X [1] [2] (b) all correct [2]; two correct [1] [2] (c) A metal cannot displace itself, so there would be no reaction and no information [1]

items.stem: Which metal would displace copper from copper sulfate solution?
items.answer: Zinc
items.markingKey: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series.

items.stem: An iron nail is placed in copper sulfate solution. What is seen?
options: A pink-brown coating forms on the nail
items.answer: A pink-brown coating forms on the nail
items.markingKey: Iron displaces copper, which coats the nail; the blue colour fades.

items.stem: Jonas adds a piece of iron to magnesium sulfate solution. What happens?
items.answer: no reaction
items.markingKey: Iron is less reactive than magnesium.

items.stem: Mohammed adds a piece of lead to silver nitrate solution. Write the word equation for the reaction.
items.answer: lead + silver nitrate → lead nitrate + silver
items.markingKey: lead nitrate [1]; silver [1] [2]

items.stem: Which metal reacts most vigorously with cold water?
items.answer: Potassium
items.markingKey: Potassium is at the top of the reactivity series.

items.stem: Explain why gold is used for jewellery that is worn every day.
items.answer: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not corrode or tarnish when in contact with air, water or sweat.
items.markingKey: unreactive [1]; does not corrode / tarnish [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why copper is used for water pipes but sodium could never be.
items.answer: Copper does not react with water; sodium reacts vigorously with water, producing hydrogen and an alkali.
items.markingKey: copper unreactive with water [1]; sodium reacts violently [1] [2]

items.stem: Chloe adds equal masses of powdered metals A, B and C to separate 25 cm³ portions of copper sulfate solution and records the temperature: metal A: 20 °C → 32 °C, metal C: 20 °C → 62 °C, metal B: 20 °C → 24 °C. Calculate the temperature rise for each metal and put the metals in order of reactivity.
items.answer: A 12 °C, C 42 °C, B 4 °C; order C > A > B
items.markingKey: temperature rises [1]; order (largest rise = most reactive) [1] [2]

items.stem: Mateo adds equal masses of powdered metals A, B and C to separate 25 cm³ portions of copper sulfate solution and records the temperature: metal C: 21 °C → 41 °C, metal B: 21 °C → 33 °C, metal A: 21 °C → 24 °C. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity. (b) Explain why a larger temperature rise shows a more reactive metal. (c) The metals are iron, lead, zinc. Identify A, B and C.
items.answer: (a) C > B > A (b) A more reactive metal reacts more vigorously with copper sulfate and releases more thermal energy (exothermic). (c) A = lead; B = iron; C = zinc
items.markingKey: (a) order [1] (b) more vigorous / more energy released [1] (c) all identified [1] [3]

items.stem: A factory in Singapore wants to store a solution of copper sulfate and also coat steel with zinc to protect it. (a) Explain why the copper sulfate solution must not be stored in a tank made of iron. (b) Explain why gold is used for electrical contacts in computers even though it is expensive.
items.answer: (a) Iron is more reactive than copper, so it would displace copper and the tank would be eaten away. (b) It is very unreactive, so it does not corrode and keeps a good electrical contact.
items.markingKey: (a) iron more reactive [1]; displaces copper / tank corrodes [1] [2] (b) unreactive / no corrosion [1]; reliable contact [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why magnesium fizzes faster than zinc in the same dilute acid.
items.answer: Magnesium is more reactive than zinc, so it reacts faster and gives off hydrogen faster.
items.markingKey: magnesium more reactive [1]; hydrogen produced faster [1] [2]

items.stem: An engineer in Bogotá is choosing metals for different jobs using the reactivity series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, copper, silver, gold. (a) Explain why potassium must never be used in contact with water. (b) Explain whether zinc would displace lead from lead nitrate solution.
items.answer: (a) It is at the top of the series and reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen that can ignite. (b) Yes: zinc is above lead in the reactivity series.
items.markingKey: (a) very reactive [1]; violent reaction / hydrogen [1] [2] (b) yes [1]; reason [1] [2]

items.stem: An engineer in Istanbul is choosing metals for different jobs using the reactivity series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, copper, silver, gold. (a) Suggest a metal from the series that could safely be used to line the tank, and explain your choice. (b) Predict how magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and write the word equation. (c) Explain whether magnesium would displace lead from lead nitrate solution.
items.answer: (a) Silver or gold (or copper itself), because they are not more reactive than copper so no displacement occurs. (b) It fizzes, giving off hydrogen. magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen (c) Yes: magnesium is above lead in the reactivity series.
items.markingKey: (a) suitable metal [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) fizzing / hydrogen [1]; word equation [1] [2] (c) yes [1]; reason [1] [2]

items.stem: What is a salt?
options: A compound that contains only non-metals
A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal
Any compound that dissolves in water
items.answer: A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal
items.markingKey: Salts form when acids react with metals, bases or carbonates.

items.stem: Explain why copper sulfate cannot be made by adding copper metal to dilute sulfuric acid.
items.answer: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids; copper oxide must be used instead.
items.markingKey: copper does not react with dilute acid [1]; use copper oxide / carbonate [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the reaction between an acid and a base is called neutralisation.
items.answer: The base cancels out the acid: the H⁺ ions of the acid react to form water, so the solution becomes neutral (pH 7).
items.markingKey: acid cancelled / water formed [1]; pH moves to 7 [1] [2]

items.stem: Write the word equation for the reaction between iron and sulfuric acid.
items.answer: iron + sulfuric acid → iron sulfate + hydrogen
items.markingKey: iron sulfate [1]; hydrogen [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya reacts zinc oxide with nitric acid. (a) Write the word equation. (b) Describe what you would see. (c) State the type of reaction.
items.answer: (a) zinc oxide + nitric acid → zinc nitrate + water (b) the solid dissolves to give a colourless solution (c) neutralisation
items.markingKey: (a) word equation [1] (b) observation [1] (c) type [1] [3]

items.stem: A class in Cairo makes iron chloride by adding iron to hydrochloric acid in excess. They start with 1 g of metal and 0.1 g remains at the end. (a) Explain why excess metal is used. (b) Describe the test for the gas given off and the result.
items.answer: (a) To make sure all the acid reacts, so the salt solution contains no leftover acid. (b) Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube: a squeaky pop shows hydrogen.
items.markingKey: (a) all acid used up [1]; pure salt solution [1] [2] (b) lighted splint [1]; squeaky pop [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why potassium is not used to make potassium chloride from hydrochloric acid in a school laboratory.
items.answer: Potassium is so reactive that it reacts violently (explosively) with acid; potassium hydroxide is used instead.
items.markingKey: violent reaction [1]; use the hydroxide instead [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila adds 1 g of magnesium to 50 cm³ of sulfuric acid until the fizzing stops. 0.1 g of magnesium is left unreacted. (a) Explain why excess metal is used. (b) Describe the test for the gas given off and the result.
items.answer: (a) To make sure all the acid reacts, so the salt solution contains no leftover acid. (b) Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube: a squeaky pop shows hydrogen.
items.markingKey: (a) all acid used up [1]; pure salt solution [1] [2] (b) lighted splint [1]; squeaky pop [1] [2]

items.stem: A class in Dhaka makes magnesium sulfate by adding magnesium to sulfuric acid in excess. They start with 1.2 g of metal and 0.24 g remains at the end. (a) Write the word equation for the reaction. (b) Explain why excess metal is used. (c) Describe how to remove the unreacted metal.
items.answer: (a) magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen (b) To make sure all the acid reacts, so the salt solution contains no leftover acid. (c) Filter the mixture; the metal stays on the filter paper and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate.
items.markingKey: (a) magnesium sulfate [1]; hydrogen [1] [2] (b) all acid used up [1]; pure salt solution [1] [2] (c) filtration [1]; metal residue, salt in filtrate [1] [2]

items.stem: What are the products when a metal carbonate reacts with an acid?
options: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
items.answer: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Explain why the mass of a flask containing marble chips and acid decreases during the reaction.
items.answer: Carbon dioxide gas is produced and escapes from the open flask, so mass is lost.
items.markingKey: carbon dioxide produced [1]; gas escapes [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how you can tell when enough copper carbonate has been added to the acid.
items.answer: No more fizzing occurs and some green solid remains undissolved (in excess).
items.markingKey: fizzing stops [1]; solid left over [1] [2]

items.stem: Write the word equation for the reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: calcium chloride [1]; water and carbon dioxide [1] [2]

items.stem: Felix puts a flask of nitric acid on a balance (total mass 112.60 g) and adds 10.00 g of zinc carbonate (the acid is in excess). When the reaction has finished the reading is 119.08 g. (a) Write the word equation. (b) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide given off. (c) Describe a test to show the gas is carbon dioxide.
items.answer: (a) zinc carbonate + nitric acid → zinc nitrate + water + carbon dioxide (b) 122.60 − 119.08 = 3.52 g (c) Bubble the gas through limewater: it turns milky.
items.markingKey: (a) equation [1] (b) 3.52 g [1] (c) limewater turns milky [1] [3]

items.stem: A school laboratory in Madrid prepares copper sulfate by reacting copper oxide with sulfuric acid. From the quantities used, 5 g of salt should form; the class obtains 3.8 g. (a) Describe how to make sure that all of the acid has reacted. (b) Suggest two reasons why the mass of crystals is less than expected.
items.answer: (a) Add copper oxide in small portions with stirring until some solid remains undissolved. (b) Some solution left on the filter paper or in the beaker; not all the salt crystallised (some stays in solution); some crystals lost when transferring.
items.markingKey: (a) add in excess [1]; solid remains / fizzing stops [1] [2] (b) any two [1] each [2]

items.stem: Which is the test for carbon dioxide?
options: It gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint
items.answer: It turns limewater milky
items.markingKey: CO₂ bubbled through limewater gives a white (milky) precipitate.

items.stem: In a test, Aisha writes: "When marble reacts with acid the mass decreases, so mass is destroyed in the reaction." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: Mass is conserved; the missing mass is carbon dioxide gas that escapes into the air.
items.markingKey: mass conserved [1]; CO₂ escapes [1] [2]

items.stem: In a chemical reaction, what happens to the atoms?
options: They are rearranged to form new substances
items.answer: They are rearranged to form new substances
items.markingKey: Atoms are not created or destroyed; they join up differently.

items.stem: Explain why the equation H₂ + O₂ → H₂O is not balanced, and balance it.
items.answer: There are 2 oxygen atoms on the left but only 1 on the right. Balanced: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
items.markingKey: oxygen atoms unequal [1]; 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a student cannot balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by writing H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂.
items.answer: Changing the subscript changes the substance: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not water; only the numbers in front can be changed.
items.markingKey: changes the substance [1]; only coefficients can change [1] [2]

items.stem: Balance this equation: Ca + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂
items.answer: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂
items.markingKey: correct numbers in front of formulae [1]; atoms equal on both sides [1] [2]

items.stem: The word equation is: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen. (a) Balance the symbol equation Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. (b) State the number of H atoms on each side of the balanced equation.
items.answer: (a) Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ (b) 2 on each side
items.markingKey: (a) balanced [2] (b) 2 [1] [3]

items.stem: The word equation is: sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen. (a) Balance the symbol equation Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂. (b) In one experiment the masses are: H₂O 7.2 g; NaOH 16 g; H₂ 0.4 g. Calculate the mass of Na.
items.answer: (a) 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ (b) 9.2 g
items.markingKey: (a) balanced [2] (b) mass of reactants = mass of products (total 16.4 g) [1]; 9.2 g [1] [4]

items.stem: In a laboratory in Lisbon, a technician carries out the reaction: sodium + chlorine → sodium chloride. (a) Balance the symbol equation Na + Cl₂ → NaCl. (b) Calculate the total mass of products formed when a total of 11.7 g of reactants react completely.
items.answer: (a) 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl (b) 11.7 g
items.markingKey: (a) correct coefficients [1]; atoms balanced [1] [2] (b) conservation of mass [1]; same mass [1] [2]

items.stem: In a laboratory in Riyadh, a technician carries out the reaction: calcium + water → calcium hydroxide + hydrogen. (a) Balance the symbol equation Ca + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. (b) Explain, in terms of atoms, why mass is conserved in this reaction. (c) State the total number of atoms in one particle of H₂O.
items.answer: (a) Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂ (b) Atoms are not created or destroyed, only rearranged into new substances, so the total mass stays the same. (c) 3
items.markingKey: (a) correct coefficients [1]; atoms balanced [1] [2] (b) atoms not created / destroyed [1]; rearranged [1] [2] (c) 3: 3 [1]

items.stem: Explain why burning magnesium in an open crucible gives a product heavier than the magnesium.
items.answer: The magnesium combines with oxygen from the air; the mass of oxygen is added to the magnesium.
items.markingKey: combines with oxygen [1]; oxygen mass added [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain what a word equation tells you that a balanced symbol equation does not, and vice versa.
items.answer: A word equation names the substances; a balanced symbol equation also shows the formulae and the numbers of each particle reacting.
items.markingKey: word: names [1]; symbol: formulae and ratios [1] [2]

items.stem: Balance this equation: H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂
items.answer: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
items.markingKey: correct numbers in front of formulae [1]; atoms equal on both sides [1] [2]

items.stem: The word equation is: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. (a) Balance the symbol equation CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. (b) In one experiment the masses are: CH₄ 16 g; CO₂ 44 g; H₂O 36 g. Calculate the mass of O₂.
items.answer: (a) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (b) 64 g
items.markingKey: (a) balanced [2] (b) mass of reactants = mass of products (total 80 g) [1]; 64 g [1] [4]

items.stem: Which pair would NOT react?
items.answer: Copper and zinc sulfate solution
items.markingKey: Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace it.

items.stem: Explain how displacement reactions can be used to place metals in order of reactivity.
items.answer: Add each metal to solutions of salts of the others; the metal that displaces the most others is the most reactive.
items.markingKey: test each metal with others’ salts [1]; more displacements = more reactive [1] [2]

items.stem: Sipho adds a piece of iron to copper sulfate solution. Write the word equation for the reaction.
items.answer: iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper
items.markingKey: iron sulfate [1]; copper [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya adds a piece of copper to lead nitrate solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs and explain your answer.
items.answer: No reaction, because copper is less reactive than lead.
items.markingKey: no reaction [1]; copper below lead in reactivity series [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Cape Town tests four unknown metals W, X, Y and Z with solutions of each other’s nitrates. Results: metal W displaced X, Y, Z; metal X displaced none of the others; metal Y displaced X, Z; metal Z displaced X. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) Explain how you used the results to decide the order.
items.answer: (a) W > Y > Z > X (b) The metal that displaced the most others is the most reactive; the one that displaced none is the least reactive.
items.markingKey: (a) W > Y > Z > X [1]; W > Y > Z > X [1] [2] (b) number of displacements [1]; most / none linked to order [1] [2]

items.stem: Which metal does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.answer: Copper
items.markingKey: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

items.stem: Explain how the reactivity series can be used to predict whether a metal reacts with dilute acid.
items.answer: Metals above hydrogen in the series react with dilute acid to give hydrogen; those below hydrogen (copper, silver, gold) do not.
items.markingKey: above hydrogen react [1]; below do not [1] [2]

items.stem: Kenji adds equal masses of powdered metals A, B and C to separate 25 cm³ portions of copper sulfate solution and records the temperature: metal A: 22 °C → 26 °C, metal C: 22 °C → 44 °C, metal B: 22 °C → 56 °C. Calculate the temperature rise for each metal and put the metals in order of reactivity.
items.answer: A 4 °C, C 22 °C, B 34 °C; order B > C > A
items.markingKey: temperature rises [1]; order (largest rise = most reactive) [1] [2]

items.stem: A factory in Kathmandu wants to store a solution of copper sulfate and also coat steel with magnesium to protect it. (a) Predict how magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and write the word equation. (b) Explain why gold is used for electrical contacts in computers even though it is expensive. (c) Explain whether magnesium would displace lead from lead nitrate solution.
items.answer: (a) It fizzes, giving off hydrogen. magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen (b) It is very unreactive, so it does not corrode and keeps a good electrical contact. (c) Yes: magnesium is above lead in the reactivity series.
items.markingKey: (a) fizzing / hydrogen [1]; word equation [1] [2] (b) unreactive / no corrosion [1]; reliable contact [1] [2] (c) yes [1]; reason [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which is the test for hydrogen gas? (b) What are the products when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid?
items.answer: (a) A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop (b) Magnesium chloride and hydrogen
items.markingKey: (a) Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop. (b) metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.

items.stem: Elena claims: "Salt just means sodium chloride." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. A salt is any compound in which the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal, e.g. copper sulfate, potassium nitrate.
items.markingKey: general definition [1]; another example [1] [2]

items.stem: Write the word equation for the reaction between zinc and sulfuric acid.
items.answer: zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen
items.markingKey: zinc sulfate [1]; hydrogen [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the acid is warmed before the copper oxide is added when making copper sulfate.
items.answer: Warming speeds up the reaction so the base reacts and dissolves faster.
items.markingKey: faster reaction [1]; base dissolves more quickly [1] [2]

items.stem: Write the word equation for the reaction between magnesium carbonate and hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: magnesium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: magnesium chloride [1]; water and carbon dioxide [1] [2]

items.stem: Felix makes crystals of copper sulfate from copper carbonate (a green solid) and dilute sulfuric acid. The expected mass of crystals is 6 g but only 4.5 g are collected. (a) Suggest two reasons why the mass of crystals is less than expected. (b) Explain why the solution is filtered before it is evaporated.
items.answer: (a) Some solution left on the filter paper or in the beaker; not all the salt crystallised (some stays in solution); some crystals lost when transferring. (b) To remove the excess unreacted copper carbonate, so the crystals are pure.
items.markingKey: (a) any two [1] each [2] (b) removes excess solid [1]; pure product [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the mass in a sealed flask stays the same when two solutions react to form a precipitate.
items.answer: No atoms enter or leave the sealed flask; they are only rearranged, so total mass is conserved.
items.markingKey: nothing escapes [1]; atoms rearranged / mass conserved [1] [2]

items.stem: In a test, Amara writes: "In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO there are more atoms on the right because the product is heavier." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: There are 2 Mg and 2 O atoms on each side; the equation is balanced and mass is conserved.
items.markingKey: atom count equal [1]; mass conserved [1] [2]

items.stem: Balance this equation: Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
items.answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
items.markingKey: correct numbers in front of formulae [1]; atoms equal on both sides [1] [2]

items.stem: In a laboratory in Nairobi, a technician carries out the reaction: copper + oxygen → copper oxide. (a) Explain, in terms of atoms, why mass is conserved in this reaction. (b) Predict what would happen to the reading on a balance if the reaction were done in a sealed flask.
items.answer: (a) Atoms are not created or destroyed, only rearranged into new substances, so the total mass stays the same. (b) It would stay the same, because no atoms can enter or leave.
items.markingKey: (a) atoms not created / destroyed [1]; rearranged [1] [2] (b) no change [1]; nothing enters or leaves [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel studies the reaction: magnesium oxide + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water. (a) Balance the symbol equation MgO + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O. (b) Predict what would happen to the reading on a balance if the reaction were done in a sealed flask. (c) State the total number of atoms in one particle of MgCl₂.
items.answer: (a) MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O (b) It would stay the same, because no atoms can enter or leave. (c) 3
items.markingKey: (a) correct coefficients [1]; atoms balanced [1] [2] (b) no change [1]; nothing enters or leaves [1] [2] (c) 3: 3 [1]

items.stem: Which is the most reactive of these metals?
items.answer: Magnesium
items.markingKey: Order: magnesium > zinc > iron > copper.

items.stem: Explain why the temperature rise is larger when magnesium, rather than iron, is added to copper sulfate solution.
items.answer: Magnesium is much further above copper than iron is, so the reaction is more vigorous and releases more energy.
items.markingKey: magnesium more reactive [1]; bigger difference in reactivity / more energy released [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar adds a piece of zinc to silver nitrate solution. Write the word equation for the reaction.
items.answer: zinc + silver nitrate → zinc nitrate + silver
items.markingKey: zinc nitrate [1]; silver [1] [2]

items.stem: Felix adds a piece of iron to zinc sulfate solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs and explain your answer.
items.answer: No reaction, because iron is less reactive than zinc.
items.markingKey: no reaction [1]; iron below zinc in reactivity series [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Muscat tests four unknown metals W, X, Y and Z with solutions of each other’s nitrates. Results: metal W displaced none of the others; metal X displaced W, Y; metal Y displaced W; metal Z displaced W, X, Y. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) The metals are iron, lead, magnesium, zinc. Suggest which letter is which metal.
items.answer: (a) Z > X > Y > W (b) W = lead; X = zinc; Y = iron; Z = magnesium
items.markingKey: (a) Z > X > Y > W [1]; Z > X > Y > W [1] [2] (b) all correct [2]; two correct [1] [2]

items.stem: Which metal is found uncombined (native) in the Earth’s crust?
items.answer: Gold
items.markingKey: Gold is so unreactive that it is found as the element.

items.stem: Suggest why the most reactive metals were discovered much later in history than gold and copper.
items.answer: Reactive metals are always found in compounds and are hard to extract; unreactive metals are found native or extracted easily.
items.markingKey: reactive metals in compounds [1]; hard to extract [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar adds equal masses of powdered metals A, B and C to separate 25 cm³ portions of copper sulfate solution and records the temperature: metal B: 22 °C → 64 °C, metal C: 22 °C → 26 °C, metal A: 22 °C → 40 °C. Calculate the temperature rise for each metal and put the metals in order of reactivity.
items.answer: B 42 °C, C 4 °C, A 18 °C; order B > A > C
items.markingKey: temperature rises [1]; order (largest rise = most reactive) [1] [2]

items.stem: A factory in Kathmandu wants to store a solution of copper sulfate and also coat steel with iron to protect it. (a) Explain why the copper sulfate solution must not be stored in a tank made of iron. (b) Predict how iron reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and write the word equation. (c) Explain why gold is used for electrical contacts in computers even though it is expensive.
items.answer: (a) Iron is more reactive than copper, so it would displace copper and the tank would be eaten away. (b) It fizzes, giving off hydrogen. iron + hydrochloric acid → iron chloride + hydrogen (c) It is very unreactive, so it does not corrode and keeps a good electrical contact.
items.markingKey: (a) iron more reactive [1]; displaces copper / tank corrodes [1] [2] (b) fizzing / hydrogen [1]; word equation [1] [2] (c) unreactive / no corrosion [1]; reliable contact [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A base that dissolves in water is called … (b) Name the salt formed when copper oxide reacts with sulfuric acid.
items.answer: (a) an alkali (b) Copper sulfate.
items.markingKey: (a) Soluble bases (e.g. sodium hydroxide) are alkalis. (b) copper sulfate [1]

items.stem: Ravi claims: "Metal oxides react with acids to give a salt and hydrogen." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. Metal oxides (bases) react with acids to give a salt and water; hydrogen is made only when a metal reacts with an acid.
items.markingKey: base + acid → salt + water [1]; hydrogen from metal + acid [1] [2]

items.stem: Write the word equation for the reaction between calcium hydroxide and sulfuric acid.
items.answer: calcium hydroxide + sulfuric acid → calcium sulfate + water
items.markingKey: calcium sulfate [1]; water [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the crystals are dried between filter papers rather than in a hot oven.
items.answer: Some salts contain water of crystallisation or decompose when heated strongly, so gentle drying keeps the crystals intact.
items.markingKey: heat can damage / decompose crystals [1]; gentle drying [1] [2]

items.stem: Write the word equation for the reaction between sodium carbonate and hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: sodium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: sodium chloride [1]; water and carbon dioxide [1] [2]

items.stem: A school laboratory in Cape Town prepares copper sulfate by reacting copper carbonate with sulfuric acid. From the quantities used, 4 g of salt should form; the class obtains 3.2 g. (a) Describe the colour change of the mixture as the copper carbonate reacts. (b) Calculate the percentage yield.
items.answer: (a) The green solid disappears and the solution becomes blue. (b) 80%
items.markingKey: (a) solid disappears [1]; solution colour [1] [2] (b) 3.2 ÷ 4 × 100 [1] = 80% [1] [2]

items.stem: How many Ca atoms are shown on the left-hand side of CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂?
items.markingKey: Multiply each subscript by the number in front: 1.

items.stem: Diego says: "A balanced equation must have the same number of molecules on each side." Explain why Diego is wrong.
items.answer: It must have the same number of each type of atom; the number of molecules can differ (e.g. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 3 then 2).
items.markingKey: atoms not molecules [1]; example [1] [2]

items.stem: Balance this equation: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
items.answer: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
items.markingKey: correct numbers in front of formulae [1]; atoms equal on both sides [1] [2]

items.stem: In a laboratory in Kuala Lumpur, a technician carries out the reaction: magnesium oxide + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water. (a) Explain, in terms of atoms, why mass is conserved in this reaction. (b) Predict what would happen to the reading on a balance if the reaction were done in a sealed flask.
items.answer: (a) Atoms are not created or destroyed, only rearranged into new substances, so the total mass stays the same. (b) It would stay the same, because no atoms can enter or leave.
items.markingKey: (a) atoms not created / destroyed [1]; rearranged [1] [2] (b) no change [1]; nothing enters or leaves [1] [2]

items.stem: In a laboratory in Hanoi, a technician carries out the reaction: sodium + oxygen → sodium oxide. (a) Calculate the total mass of products formed when a total of 62 g of reactants react completely. (b) Predict what would happen to the reading on a balance if the reaction were done in a sealed flask. (c) State the total number of atoms in one particle of Na₂O.
items.answer: (a) 62 g (b) It would stay the same, because no atoms can enter or leave. (c) 3
items.markingKey: (a) conservation of mass [1]; same mass [1] [2] (b) no change [1]; nothing enters or leaves [1] [2] (c) 3: 3 [1]
